claim: Intraflagellar transport (IFT) carries proteins into flagella.
source: Intraflagellar transport (IFT) carries proteins into flagella but how IFT trains interact with the large number of diverse proteins required to assemble flagella remains largely unknown.
evidence: This is a well-established concept in the field, stated in the abstract.

claim: IFT of radial spokes in Chlamydomonas requires ARMC2/PF27.
source: Here, we show that IFT of radial spokes in Chlamydomonas requires ARMC2/PF27, a conserved armadillo repeat protein associated with male infertility and reduced lung function.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments including imaging and mutant analysis.

claim: ARMC2 is a conserved armadillo repeat protein associated with male infertility and reduced lung function.
source: Here, we show that IFT of radial spokes in Chlamydomonas requires ARMC2/PF27, a conserved armadillo repeat protein associated with male infertility and reduced lung function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on mammalian ARMC2.

claim: Chlamydomonas ARMC2 was highly enriched in growing flagella.
source: Chlamydomonas ARMC2 was highly enriched in growing flagella and tagged ARMC2 and the spoke protein RSP3 co-migrated on anterograde trains.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot analysis and TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Tagged ARMC2 and the spoke protein RSP3 co-migrated on anterograde trains.
source: Chlamydomonas ARMC2 was highly enriched in growing flagella and tagged ARMC2 and the spoke protein RSP3 co-migrated on anterograde trains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by two-color TIRF imaging in Figure 3.

claim: A cargo and an adapter of inner and outer dynein arms moved independently of ARMC2.
source: In contrast, a cargo and an adapter of inner and outer dynein arms moved independently of ARMC2, indicating that unrelated cargoes distribute stochastically onto the IFT trains.
evidence: This is supported by two-color imaging experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Unrelated cargoes distribute stochastically onto the IFT trains.
source: In contrast, a cargo and an adapter of inner and outer dynein arms moved independently of ARMC2, indicating that unrelated cargoes distribute stochastically onto the IFT trains.
evidence: This is inferred from the independent movement of different cargoes and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: After concomitant unloading at the flagellar tip, RSP3 attached to the axoneme whereas ARMC2 diffused back to the cell body.
source: After concomitant unloading at the flagellar tip, RSP3 attached to the axoneme whereas ARMC2 diffused back to the cell body.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: In armc2/pf27 mutants, IFT of radial spokes was abolished.
source: In armc2/pf27 mutants, IFT of radial spokes was abolished and the presence of radial spokes was limited to the proximal region of flagella.
evidence: This is shown by TIRF imaging in Figure 3D where RSP3-NG transport by IFT was not observed in armc2 mutants.

claim: The presence of radial spokes was limited to the proximal region of flagella in armc2/pf27 mutants.
source: In armc2/pf27 mutants, IFT of radial spokes was abolished and the presence of radial spokes was limited to the proximal region of flagella.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and TIRF imaging in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: ARMC2 is a cargo adapter required for IFT of radial spokes to ensure their assembly along flagella.
source: We conclude that ARMC2 is a cargo adapter required for IFT of radial spokes to ensure their assembly along flagella.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: ARMC2 belongs to a growing class of cargo-specific adapters that enable flagellar transport of preassembled axonemal substructures by IFT.
source: ARMC2 belongs to a growing class of cargo-specific adapters that enable flagellar transport of preassembled axonemal substructures by IFT.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with other known adapters like ODA16 and IDA3.

claim: Cilia and eukaryotic flagella consist of hundreds of distinct proteins, which are synthesized in the cell body and moved posttranslationally into the organelle.
source: Cilia and eukaryotic flagella consist of hundreds of distinct proteins, which are synthesized in the cell body and moved posttranslationally into the organelle (Rosenbaum and Child, 1967; Pazour et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Protein transport into flagella involves intraflagellar transport (IFT), a motor-based bidirectional motility of protein carriers.
source: Protein transport into flagella involves intraflagellar transport (IFT), a motor-based bidirectional motility of protein carriers (i.e., 'IFT trains') (Kozminski et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Numerous proteins of the flagellar axoneme, matrix, and membrane have been shown to use the IFT pathway for flagellar entry and exit.
source: Numerous proteins of the flagellar axoneme, matrix, and membrane have been shown to use the IFT pathway for flagellar entry and exit (Lechtreck, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: IFT trains are composed of just 22 IFT proteins and the associated kinesin-2 and IFT dynein motors.
source: This raises the question how IFT trains, composed of just 22 IFT proteins and the associated kinesin-2 and IFT dynein motors, interact with the large number of diverse flagellar proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IFT train composition.

claim: Tubulin binds directly to the N-terminal domains of the IFT-B core proteins IFT74 and IFT81.
source: Tubulin, the most abundant flagellar protein, binds directly to the N-terminal domains of the IFT-B core proteins IFT74 and IFT81 (Bhogaraju et al., 2013; Craft et al., 2015; Kubo et al., 2016; Craft Van De Weghe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Many proteins do not bind directly to the IFT trains but the interaction is mediated by IFT cargo adapters.
source: However, many other proteins do not bind directly to the IFT trains but the interaction is mediated by IFT cargo adapters.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The octameric BBSome acts as a linker for a diverse group of transmembrane and membrane-associated proteins, attaching them indirectly to IFT trains.
source: The octameric BBSome, for example, acts as a linker for a diverse group of transmembrane and membrane-associated proteins, attaching them indirectly to IFT trains (Nachury et al., 2007; Liu and Lechtreck, 2018; Wingfield et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: IFT of outer dynein arms (ODAs) requires the adapter protein ODA16.
source: With respect to axonemal proteins, IFT of outer dynein arms (ODAs) and the inner dynein arm (IDA) I1/f requires the adapter proteins ODA16 and IDA3, respectively (Ahmed et al., 2008; Dai et al., 2018; Hunter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: IFT of the inner dynein arm (IDA) I1/f requires the adapter protein IDA3.
source: With respect to axonemal proteins, IFT of outer dynein arms (ODAs) and the inner dynein arm (IDA) I1/f requires the adapter proteins ODA16 and IDA3, respectively (Ahmed et al., 2008; Dai et al., 2018; Hunter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The oda16 and ida3 mutants assemble full-length flagella that specifically lack ODAs or IDAs I1/f, respectively, but of otherwise normal ultrastructure.
source: The corresponding oda16 and ida3 mutants assemble full-length flagella that specifically lack ODAs or IDAs I1/f, respectively, but of otherwise normal ultrastructure (Ahmed and Mitchell, 2005; Hunter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: ODAs and IDAs are large multiprotein complexes, which are assembled in the cell body before the entire substructures are moved into the flagella by IFT.
source: ODAs and IDAs are large multiprotein complexes, which are assembled in the cell body before the entire substructures are moved into the flagella by IFT (Fowkes and Mitchell, 1998; King, 2012; Viswanadha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: More than 20 radial spoke (RS) proteins preassemble into a 12S RS precursor in the cell body.
source: Similarly, more than 20 radial spoke (RS) proteins preassemble into a 12S RS precursor in the cell body (Qin et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The L-shaped RS precursors are moved by IFT to the flagellar tip, converted into the mature 20S spoke complexes, and assembled as T-shaped spokes onto the axonemal doublets.
source: Then, the L-shaped precursors are moved by IFT to the flagellar tip, converted into the mature 20S spoke complexes, and assembled as T-shaped spokes onto the axonemal doublets (Qin et al., 2004; Diener et al., 2011; Lechtreck et al., 2018; Grossman-Haham et al., 2021; Gui et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Mutations in the genes encoding the various spoke subunits lead to partial or complete loss of the RSs and flagellar paralysis.
source: Mutations in the genes encoding the various spoke subunits lead to partial or complete loss of the RSs and flagellar paralysis (Luck et al., 1977; Piperno et al., 1977; Witman et al., 1978; Piperno et al., 1981; Curry and Rosenbaum, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The pf27 mutant assembles RSs of normal ultrastructure and subunit composition but the presence of spokes is limited to the very proximal region of the mutant flagella.
source: The pf27 mutant, however, stands out as it assembles RSs of normal ultrastructure and subunit composition but the presence of spokes is limited to the very proximal region of the mutant flagella (Huang et al., 1981; Alford et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In vitro decoration experiments revealed that the pf27 axonemes bind control and pf27 spokes, indicating that axonemal docking of RSs is unaffected in pf27.
source: In vitro decoration experiments using isolated axonemes and RSs revealed that the pf27 axonemes bind control and pf27 spokes, indicating that axonemal docking of RSs is unaffected in pf27 (Alford et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Alford et al., 2013, postulated that PF27 could encode a factor required for the transport of RSs into the distal flagellum via IFT.
source: To explain the absence of spokes from large sections of the pf27 flagella, Alford et al., 2013, postulated that PF27 could encode a factor required for the transport of RSs into the distal flagellum via IFT.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a previous study.

claim: RS assembly in the proximal region of pf27 flagella could result from residual entry of RSs by diffusion followed by binding to the nearest available docking sites.
source: Then, RS assembly in the proximal region of pf27 flagella could result from residual entry of RSs by diffusion followed by binding to the nearest available docking sites.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed phenotype.

claim: It has been proposed that phosphorylation of RS proteins occurs near the flagellar tip.
source: Such a scenario could also explain why the phosphorylation state of several RS proteins is altered in pf27 as it has been proposed that phosphorylation of these proteins occurs near the flagellar tip, which the RSs would fail to reach in pf27 (Huang et al., 1981; Yang and Yang, 2006; Gupta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous studies.

claim: The pf27 mutation maps close to the centromere of chromosome 12.
source: The pf27 mutation maps close to the centromere of chromosome 12 but, despite whole genomes sequencing approaches, the PF27 gene product remained unknown (Kathir et al., 2003; Alford et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Despite whole genomes sequencing approaches, the PF27 gene product remained unknown prior to this study.
source: The pf27 mutation maps close to the centromere of chromosome 12 but, despite whole genomes sequencing approaches, the PF27 gene product remained unknown (Kathir et al., 2003; Alford et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: ARMC2 encodes an armadillo repeat protein conserved in organisms with motile cilia.
source: Cre12.g559300 encodes the armadillo repeat protein ARMC2 (annotated as ARM1 in Phytozome), which is conserved in organisms with motile cilia (Li et al., 2004; Merchant et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The mammalian homologue of ARMC2 has been linked to reduced lung function and male infertility.
source: The mammalian homologue of ARMC2 has been linked to reduced lung function and male infertility but the precise role of ARMC2 in the assembly of motile cilia remained unknown (Soler Artigas et al., 2011; Coutton et al., 2019; Pereira et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The precise role of ARMC2 in the assembly of motile cilia remained unknown prior to this study.
source: The mammalian homologue of ARMC2 has been linked to reduced lung function and male infertility but the precise role of ARMC2 in the assembly of motile cilia remained unknown (Soler Artigas et al., 2011; Coutton et al., 2019; Pereira et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: A novel Chlamydomonas armc2 mutant shares the RS-deficient phenotype of pf27.
source: A novel Chlamydomonas armc2 mutant shares the RS-deficient phenotype of p27.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot and imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of ARMC2 restored wild-type motility and the presence of RSs in both armc2 and pf27 flagella.
source: Expression of ARMC2 restored wild-type motility and the presence of RSs in both armc2 and pf27 flagella, revealing that PF27 encodes ARMC2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: PF27 encodes ARMC2.
source: Expression of ARMC2 restored wild-type motility and the presence of RSs in both armc2 and pf27 flagella, revealing that PF27 encodes ARMC2.
evidence: This is concluded from the rescue experiments.

claim: IFT of RSP3 was abolished in armc2.
source: Fluorescent protein (FP)-tagged ARMC2 and the RS subunit RSP3 co-migrate on anterograde IFT trains in regenerating Chlamydomonas flagella whereas IFT of RSP3 was abolished in armc2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging in Figure 3D.

claim: IFT of ODAs, IDAs I1/f, and RSs, three large axonemal substructures pre-assembled in the cell body, requires adapters with single cargo specificity.
source: Thus, IFT of ODAs, IDAs I1/f, and RSs, three large axonemal substructures pre-assembled in the cell body, requires adapters with single cargo specificity.
evidence: This is inferred from the data on ARMC2, ODA16, and IDA3.

claim: These adapters enter flagella and bind to IFT in the absence of their respective cargoes.
source: As these adapters enter flagella and bind to IFT in the absence of their respective cargoes, we propose that the regulation of IFT-adapter interaction is a critical step for controlling cargo import into flagella by IFT.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging ARMC2 in pf14 mutants (Figure 2).

claim: The regulation of IFT-adapter interaction is a critical step for controlling cargo import into flagella by IFT.
source: As these adapters enter flagella and bind to IFT in the absence of their respective cargoes, we propose that the regulation of IFT-adapter interaction is a critical step for controlling cargo import into flagella by IFT.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental observations.

claim: The pf27 locus was mapped to the midpoint between the ODA9 and TUB2 locus near the centromeric region of chromosome 12.
source: The pf27 locus was mapped to the midpoint between the ODA9 and TUB2 locus near the centromeric region of chromosome 12, placing it in the vicinity of the Cre12.g559250 gene, which encodes a 14-3-3 protein (Kathir et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Cre12.g559300 was identified as a potential candidate for PF27.
source: In the Phytozome genome browser (https://phytozome.jgi.doe.gov/pz/portal.html), we inspected this region for genes with a predicted role in flagella and identified Cre12.g559300 as a potential candidate.
evidence: This describes the candidate approach used in the study.

claim: From the CLiP library, the mutant strains LMJ.RY0402.155726 and LMJ.RY0402.083979 were obtained, which have insertions in the 11th and last intron of Cre12.g559300, respectively.
source: From the CLiP library we obtained the mutant strains LMJ.RY0402.155726 and LMJ.RY0402.083979, which have insertions in the 11th and last intron of Cre12.g559300, respectively (Figure 1A; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1A and citation.

claim: Strain LMJ.RY0402.155726 had paralyzed flagella displaying residual jerky movements resembling pf27.
source: Strain LMJ.RY0402.155726 had paralyzed flagella displaying residual jerky movements resembling pf27 and we refer to this strain as armc2 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by motility analysis in Figure 1B.

claim: Western blot analysis showed reduced levels of the RS proteins RSP3 and nucleoside diphosphate kinase 5 (NDK5 aka RSP23) in flagella of armc2 and pf27.
source: Western blot analysis showed reduced levels of the RS proteins RSP3 and nucleoside diphosphate kinase 5 (NDK5 aka RSP23) in flagella of armc2 and pf27 (Figure 1C, D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 1C, D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In comparison to wild-type flagella, the slower migrating phosphorylated forms of RS proteins were less abundant in armc2 flagella.
source: In comparison to wild-type flagella, the slower migrating phosphorylated forms of these proteins, which can be separated by long runs on 6% acrylamide gels, were less abundant in armc2 flagella, as previously described for pf27 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Huang et al., 1981).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and supported by citation.

claim: In control cells, RSP3-NG is present essentially along the length of flagella.
source: In control cells, RSP3-NG is present essentially along the length of flagella (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Lechtreck et al., 2018).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and supported by citation.

claim: RSP3-NG was concentrated in the proximal region of the armc2 flagella; it then tapered off and was largely absent from a large distal segment of flagella.
source: In contrast, RSP3-NG was concentrated in the proximal region of the armc2 flagella; it then tapered off and was largely absent from a large distal segment of flagella, similar to observations in pf27 (Figure 1E a–f, F d–f, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Alford et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging in Figure 1E and 1F and supported by citation.

claim: armc2 and pf27 flagella share the same RS-related biochemical, structural, and functional defects.
source: In conclusion, armc2 and pf27 flagella share the same RS-related biochemical, structural, and functional defects.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparative analysis of the two mutants.

claim: Chlamydomonas ARMC2 is predicted to encode a 107 kD protein.
source: Chlamydomonas ARMC2 is predicted to encode a 107 kD protein.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Mass spectrometry of affinity-purified ARMC2-3xTAG was used to confirm the coding sequence of ARMC2.
source: Mass spectrometry of affinity-purified ARMC2-3xTAG was used to confirm the coding sequence of ARMC2.
evidence: This is described in the methods and results.

claim: The purified ARMC2-3xTAG fusion protein migrated at ~160 kD in Western blots, consistent with its predicted size.
source: The purified fusion protein migrated at ~160 kD in Western blots, consistent with its predicted size (107 and 34 kD for the tag; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A total of 17 unique ARMC2 peptides were identified using Ni-NTA-purification from whole cell extracts and anti-NG-nanobody trap purification from flagellar extracts.
source: Using Ni-NTA-purification from whole cell extracts and anti-NG-nanobody trap purification from flagellar extracts, we identified a total of 17 unique ARMC2 peptides.
evidence: This is described in the results.

claim: The experimental peptides covered 42% of the predicted ARMC2 protein and were distributed through all but 1 of the 17 predicted ARMC2 exons.
source: Together with additional peptides obtained by mining other proteomic studies (Zhao et al., 2019; Picariello et al., 2020), the experimental peptides covered 42% of the predicted protein and were distributed through all but 1 (i.e., the 14th) of the 17 predicted ARMC2 exons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and supported by citations.

claim: Chlamydomonas and human ARMC2 are reciprocal best hits in protein BLAST searches with an E value of 4E-50.
source: Chlamydomonas and human ARMC2 are reciprocal best hits in protein BLAST searches with an E value of 4E-50.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The N-terminal ~400 residues of ARMC2 are predicted to be mostly intrinsically disordered by IUPred2A.
source: The N-terminal ~400 residues of ARMC2 (~300 residues of the smaller human Armc2 isoform CRA_b) are predicted to be mostly intrinsically disordered by IUPred2A (IUPred2A (elte.hu)) and include the 10 phospho-sites identified by phosphoproteomics (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F) (Wang et al., 2014; Erdős and Dosztányi, 2020).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and supported by citations.

claim: The N-terminal region of ARMC2 includes the 10 phospho-sites identified by phosphoproteomics.
source: The N-terminal ~400 residues of ARMC2 (~300 residues of the smaller human Armc2 isoform CRA_b) are predicted to be mostly intrinsically disordered by IUPred2A (IUPred2A (elte.hu)) and include the 10 phospho-sites identified by phosphoproteomics (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F) (Wang et al., 2014; Erdős and Dosztányi, 2020).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and supported by citation.

claim: The C-terminal ~600 residues of ARMC2 are predicted to be largely α-helical and encompass three armadillo repeats.
source: The C-terminal ~600 residues of ARMC2 are predicted to be largely α-helical and encompass three armadillo repeats.
evidence: This is based on structural prediction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The authors failed to identify the causal genetic defect in pf27 by sequencing of genomic PCR products.
source: Similar to previous efforts using whole genome sequencing, we failed to identify the causal genetic defect in pf27 by sequencing of genomic PCR products; a possible contributing factor is the highly repetitive nature of the centromeric DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: A possible contributing factor to the failure to identify the pf27 mutation is the highly repetitive nature of the centromeric DNA.
source: Similar to previous efforts using whole genome sequencing, we failed to identify the causal genetic defect in pf27 by sequencing of genomic PCR products; a possible contributing factor is the highly repetitive nature of the centromeric DNA.
evidence: This is speculation about the technical difficulty.

claim: In full-length flagella, only few ARMC2-3xTAG particles were observed moving by diffusion and, occasionally, by anterograde IFT.
source: In full-length flagella, we observed only few ARMC2-3xTAG particles moving by diffusion and, occasionally, by anterograde IFT (0.9 IFT events/min/flagellum, SD 1.6 events/min/flagellum, n = 16; Figure 2Aa, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging in Figure 2A and quantified in Figure 2B.

claim: Anterograde IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG was frequent in regenerating flagella with an average transport frequency of 44 events/min/flagellum.
source: In contrast, anterograde IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG was frequent in regenerating flagella with an average transport frequency of 44 events/min/flagellum (SD 16.2 events/min/flagellum, n = 34) approaching those observed for GFP-tagged IFT itself (~60–80/min; Figure 2Ab, B) (Kozminski et al., 1993; Reck et al., 2016; Wingfield et al., 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging in Figure 2A and quantified in Figure 2B, with comparison to cited IFT frequencies.

claim: ARMC2-3xTAG moved in one processive run from the flagellar base to the tip by anterograde IFT with an average velocity of 1.71 µm/s.
source: Typically, ARMC2-3xTAG moved in one processive run from the flagellar base to the tip by anterograde IFT with an average velocity of 1.71 µm/s (SD 0.24 µm/s, N = 65 particles; green arrowheads in Figure 2C a–c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by kymogram analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: ARMC2-3xTAG dwelled at the flagellar tip on average for 2.3 s.
source: As previously described for IFT proteins and other cargoes, ARMC2-3xTAG dwelled at the flagellar tip on average for 2.3 s (SD 1.8 s, n = 67; white brackets in Figure 2C a–c) (Wren et al., 2013; Chien et al., 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by kymogram analysis in Figure 2C and supported by citations.

claim: Dwelling and high-frequency transport resulted in the formation of a pool of ARMC2-3xTAG at the tip of regenerating flagella.
source: Dwelling and high-frequency transport resulted in the formation of a pool of ARMC2-3xTAG at the tip of regenerating flagella (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Once released from IFT, ARMC2-3xTAG diffused swiftly into the flagellar shaft.
source: Once released from IFT, ARMC2-3xTAG diffused swiftly into the flagellar shaft (white arrowheads in Figure 2C a–c; Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by kymogram analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: Retrograde IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG was rare.
source: Retrograde IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG was rare (Figure 2B, red arrow in Figure 2C d) indicating that the protein returns mostly by diffusion to the cell body as previously described for the anterograde IFT motor kinesin-2 and IDA3, the cargo adapter for IDA I1/f (Chien et al., 2017; Hunter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and 2C and supported by citations.

claim: ARMC2-3xTAG returns mostly by diffusion to the cell body.
source: Retrograde IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG was rare (Figure 2B, red arrow in Figure 2C d) indicating that the protein returns mostly by diffusion to the cell body as previously described for the anterograde IFT motor kinesin-2 and IDA3, the cargo adapter for IDA I1/f (Chien et al., 2017; Hunter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the rare retrograde IFT and supported by citations.

claim: Typically, ARMC2-3xTAG bleached in a single step indicating that only a single copy of the tagged protein was present on an individual IFT train.
source: Typically, ARMC2-3xTAG bleached in a single step indicating that only a single copy of the tagged protein was present on an individual IFT train (dashed circle in Figure 2C b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by photobleaching analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: Trains carrying two copies of ARMC2-3xTAG were also observed.
source: However, trains carrying two copies of ARMC2-3xTAG were also observed (Figure 2C e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C e.

claim: ARMC2-3xTAG was enriched about 14× in regenerating flagella compared to full-length flagella when a similar number of flagella were loaded.
source: When a similar number of flagella, that is, one regenerating for each full-length flagellum, were loaded, ARMC2-3xTAG was enriched about 14× in the regenerating flagella (Figure 2E, lanes 1 and 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 2E and quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The amount of IFT proteins in flagella is largely independent of flagellar length.
source: In contrast, the IFT particle protein IFT54 was similarly abundant in both samples, in agreement with previous observations that the amount of IFT proteins in flagella is largely independent of flagellar length (Marshall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: When approximately similar amounts of protein were loaded, both IFT54 and especially tagged ARMC2 were enriched in regenerating flagella.
source: When approximately similar amounts of protein were loaded, that is, several short flagella for each full-length flagellum, both IFT54 and especially tagged ARMC2 were enriched in regenerating flagella (Figure 2E, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 2E.

claim: ARMC2 is highly enriched in growing flagella.
source: Thus, ARMC2 is highly enriched in growing flagella.
evidence: This is concluded from the Western blot analysis.

claim: ARMC2-3xTAG moved by IFT in pf14 flagella.
source: ARMC2-3xTAG moved by IFT in pf14 flagella and the frequency of its transport was upregulated in regenerating pf14 flagella (Figure 2A c and d, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging in Figure 2A and quantified in Figure 2B.

claim: The frequency of ARMC2-3xTAG transport was upregulated in regenerating pf14 flagella.
source: ARMC2-3xTAG moved by IFT in pf14 flagella and the frequency of its transport was upregulated in regenerating pf14 flagella (Figure 2A c and d, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging in Figure 2A and quantified in Figure 2B.

claim: IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG and its regulation by flagellar length do not require the presence of RSP3.
source: In conclusion, IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG and its regulation by flagellar length do not require the presence of RSP3.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that ARMC2 moves by IFT in pf14 mutants lacking RSP3.

claim: IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG during flagellar regeneration in the pf14 background was notably less frequent than in cells with intact RSs.
source: IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG during flagellar regeneration in the pf14 background, however, was notably less frequent than in cells with intact RSs (Figure 2A and B) and Western blot analysis of whole cell samples showed similar amounts of ARMC2-3xTAG in the pf27 ARMC2-3xTAG rescue strain and the pf14 armc2 ARMC2-3xTAG strain (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging in Figure 2A and quantified in Figure 2B, with Western blot in Figure 2F.

claim: Western blot analysis of whole cell samples showed similar amounts of ARMC2-3xTAG in the pf27 ARMC2-3xTAG rescue strain and the pf14 armc2 ARMC2-3xTAG strain.
source: IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG during flagellar regeneration in the pf14 background, however, was notably less frequent than in cells with intact RSs (Figure 2A and B) and Western blot analysis of whole cell samples showed similar amounts of ARMC2-3xTAG in the pf27 ARMC2-3xTAG rescue strain and the pf14 armc2 ARMC2-3xTAG strain (Figure 2F).

claim: The presence of intact RSs could promote IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG.

claim: pf14 flagella regenerate slower than those of wild-type strains and accumulated IFT proteins.
source: However, similar to other strains with large structural defects in the axoneme, pf14 flagella regenerate slower than those of wild-type strains and accumulated IFT proteins (Figure 1C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and not shown) (Lechtreck et al., 2013).

evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation.

claim: In growing flagella, ARMC2-3xTAG moves on anterograde IFT trains.

evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging in Figure 3A and supported by citation.

claim: RSs are transported more frequently during flagellar growth.
source: In growing flagella, ARMC2-3xTAG moves on anterograde IFT trains suggesting that it could assist in IFT of RSs, which are also transported more frequently during flagellar growth (Figure 3A and B; Lechtreck et al., 2018).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and supported by citation.

claim: 104 (80%) of 130 observed RSP3-NG anterograde transports were accompanied by ARMC2-mS.
source: In detail, 104 (80%) of 130 observed RSP3-NG anterograde transports observed over 1622 s in 20 regenerating flagella were accompanied by ARMC2-mS (Figure 3A and C, Table 1).
evidence: This is quantified from two-color TIRF imaging shown in Figure 3A and summarized in Figure 3C and Table 1.

claim: ~82% of the ARMC2 transports were not accompanied by an RSP3-NG signal.
source: In contrast, ~82% of the ARMC2 transport were not accompanied by an RSP3-NG signal showing that ARMC2-mS transports were considerably more frequent than those of RSP3-NG in both full-length and regenerating flagella (Figure 3A and C, Table 1).
evidence: This is quantified from two-color TIRF imaging shown in Figure 3A and summarized in Figure 3C and Table 1.

claim: ARMC2-mS transports were considerably more frequent than those of RSP3-NG in both full-length and regenerating flagella.
source: In contrast, ~82% of the ARMC2 transport were not accompanied by an RSP3-NG signal showing that ARMC2-mS transports were considerably more frequent than those of RSP3-NG in both full-length and regenerating flagella (Figure 3A and C, Table 1).
evidence: This is quantified from two-color TIRF imaging shown in Figure 3A and summarized in Figure 3C and Table 1.

claim: Some ARMC2-mS was likely photobleached during the preparatory step of photobleaching axonemal RSP3-NG.
source: With respect to RSP3-NG transports lacking an ARMC2-mS signal, we note that in order to visualize IFT of RSP3-NG, we first had to photobleach the substantial amounts of RSP3-NG already incorporated into the axoneme. As mS is less photostable than NG, it is likely that some ARMC2-mS was photobleached during this preparatory step probably explaining the occurrence of some RSP3-NG transports without a co-migrating ARMC2-mS signal.
evidence: This is speculation about a technical limitation.

claim: RSP3-NG co-migrates with ARMC2-mS during anterograde IFT but the transport frequency of ARMC2-mS exceeds that of its RSP3-NG.
source: To conclude, RSP3-NG co-migrates with ARMC2-mS during anterograde IFT but the transport frequency of ARMC2-mS exceeds that of its RSP3-NG.
evidence: This is concluded from the two-color imaging data.

claim: Some RSP3-NG particles moved inside flagella by diffusion in armc2 pf14 double mutant.
source: Some RSP3-NG particles moved inside flagella by diffusion and, as flagella elongated, the amount of RSP3-NG anchored in the proximal flagellar region increased (Figure 3D d–j) (Alford et al., 2013).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and supported by citation.

claim: As flagella elongated in armc2 pf14 double mutant, the amount of RSP3-NG anchored in the proximal flagellar region increased.
source: Some RSP3-NG particles moved inside flagella by diffusion and, as flagella elongated, the amount of RSP3-NG anchored in the proximal flagellar region increased (Figure 3D d–j) (Alford et al., 2013).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and supported by citation.

claim: Transport of RSP3-NG by IFT was not observed in the armc2 mutant background.
source: But for rare ambiguous events, transport of RSP3-NG by IFT was not observed in the armc2 mutant background (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging in Figure 3D.

claim: ARMC2 is required for IFT of RSs.
source: We conclude that ARMC2 is required for IFT of RSs.
evidence: This is concluded from the absence of RSP3-NG IFT in armc2 mutants.

claim: ARMC2 is largely absent from full-length flagella while RSs are retained.
source: ARMC2 is largely absent from full-length flagella while RSs are retained, indicating that the two will separate after cotransport.
evidence: This is inferred from the imaging and Western blot data.

claim: ARMC2 and RSP3 separate after cotransport.
source: ARMC2 is largely absent from full-length flagella while RSs are retained, indicating that the two will separate after cotransport.
evidence: This is inferred from the imaging and Western blot data.

claim: The release of ARMC2-mS from its dwell phase at the tip occurred concurrently with the onset of RSP3-NG movements.
source: The analysis of 15 such ARMC2-mS RSP3-NG complexes showed that the release of ARMC2-mS from its dwell phase at the tip occurred concurrently with the onset of RSP3-NG movements (white arrowheads in Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by kymogram analysis in Figure 4.

claim: While ARMC2-mS mostly diffused into the flagellar shaft, RSP3-NG moved to a somewhat more subdistal position, where it typically remained stationary for extended periods of time.
source: While ARMC2-mS mostly diffused into the flagellar shaft, RSP3-NG moved to a somewhat more subdistal position, where it typically remained stationary for extended periods of time (12 of 15 events) potentially indicating stable docking to the axoneme.
evidence: This is demonstrated by kymogram analysis in Figure 4.

claim: RSP3-NG remaining stationary at a subdistal position potentially indicates stable docking to the axoneme.
source: While ARMC2-mS mostly diffused into the flagellar shaft, RSP3-NG moved to a somewhat more subdistal position, where it typically remained stationary for extended periods of time (12 of 15 events) potentially indicating stable docking to the axoneme.
evidence: This is speculation about the meaning of the observed behavior.

claim: ARMC2 and RSP3 separate after arrival and dwelling at the tip with RSP3 remaining in the flagellum and ARMC2 returning to the cell body.
source: Thus, ARMC2 and RSP3 separate after arrival and dwelling at the tip with RSP3 remaining in the flagellum and ARMC2 returning to the cell body.
evidence: This is concluded from the kymogram analysis in Figure 4.

claim: The frequency of ARMC2-3xTAG transport by IFT is upregulated in short growing flagella.
source: The frequency of ARMC2-3xTAG transport by IFT is upregulated in short growing flagella.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the long-short cell experiments in Figure 5.

claim: In all 19 pf27 ARMC2-3xTAG long-short cells analyzed, the IFT frequency of ARMC2-3xTAG in the shorter flagellum exceeded that of the longer flagellum.
source: In all 19 pf27 ARMC2-3xTAG long-short cells analyzed, the IFT frequency of ARMC2-3xTAG in the shorter flagellum exceeded that of the longer flagellum (on average 29.1 events/min, SD 16 events/min for the shorter vs. 8.9 events/min, SD 6.8 events/min for the longer flagellum; Figure 5A and B; Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging in Figure 5A and quantified in Figure 5B.

claim: As the length difference between the short and long flagellum decreased, the difference in ARMC2-3xTAG transport frequency between the two flagella also diminished.
source: As the length difference between the short and long flagellum decreased, the difference in ARMC2-3xTAG transport frequency between the two flagella also diminished (Figure 5A c and d, B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Flagellum-autonomous regulation of transport frequency by flagellar length was previously documented for GFP-tubulin, DRC4-GFP, and the cargo adapter IDA3.
source: A similar behavior, that is, flagellum-autonomous regulation of transport frequency by flagellar length, was previously documented for GFP-tubulin, DRC4-GFP, and the cargo adapter IDA3 (Craft et al., 2015; Hunter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The frequency of anterograde ARMC2-3xTAG transport in the shorter flagellum exceeded that of the longer flagellum of the same cell in all 14 long-short cells analyzed in the presence of cycloheximide.
source: The frequency of anterograde ARMC2-3xTAG transport in the shorter flagellum exceeded that of the longer flagellum of the same cell in all 14 long-short cells analyzed with average transport frequencies of 33 events/min (SD 13.2 events/min, n = 14) and 10.2 events/min (SD 8.1 events/min, n = 14) for short and long flagella, respectively (Figure 5C, Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF imaging and quantified in Figure 5C.

claim: ARMC2-3xTAG anterograde transport in regenerating short flagella is approximately 4× more frequent than in the longer flagella of the same cell regardless of the cycloheximide treatment.
source: Thus, ARMC2-3xTAG anterograde transport in regenerating short flagella is approximately 4× more frequent than in the longer flagella of the same cell regardless of the cycloheximide treatment.
evidence: This is concluded from the cycloheximide experiments.

claim: In cells deflagellated in the presence of CHX and allowed to regrow flagella in the presence of CHX for 90 min, the frequency of ARMC2-3xTAG transport was 14.4 events/min.
source: We also deflagellated cells by a pH shock in the presence of CHX and allowed them to regrow flagella in the presence of 10 µg/ml CHX for 90 min, at which point the flagella are approximately half-length and elongation had ceased due to the absence of protein synthesis (Rosenbaum et al., 1969). In such cells, the frequency of ARMC2-3xTAG transport was 14.4 events/min (SD 4.3, n = 10) well above the frequency determined for full-length flagella (see Figure 2B).
evidence: This is described in the results and supported by citation.

claim: High-frequency ARMC2-3xTAG transport is triggered by the insufficient length of the flagella rather than active growth of flagella.
source: Thus, high-frequency ARMC2-3xTAG transport is indeed triggered by the insufficient length of the flagella rather than active growth of flagella.
evidence: This is concluded from the cycloheximide experiments.

claim: Cells possess a pool of ARMC2-3xTAG.
source: Taken together, the data indicate that cells possess a pool of ARMC2-3xTAG and that ARMC2-3xTAG will preferably attach to IFT trains that enter short flagella.
evidence: This is inferred from the cycloheximide experiments and imaging data.

claim: ARMC2-3xTAG will preferably attach to IFT trains that enter short flagella.
source: Taken together, the data indicate that cells possess a pool of ARMC2-3xTAG and that ARMC2-3xTAG will preferably attach to IFT trains that enter short flagella.
evidence: This is inferred from the length-dependent regulation of ARMC2 transport.

claim: An ARMC2-mS pool was present near the flagellar base of most cells.
source: To determine its distribution, we analyzed pf14 armc2 RSP3-NG ARMC2-mS cells using epifluorescence, which revealed the presence of an ARMC2-mS pool near the flagellar base of most cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ARMC2-3xTAG pool typically consisted of two closely spaced dots.
source: The ARMC2-3xTAG pool typically consisted of two closely spaced dots and we use a focused laser beam to photobleach one of the two dots (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Recovery of the ARMC2-3xTAG signal after photobleaching was incomplete and plateaued after ~20 s.
source: Analysis of a small number of pf27 ARMC2-3xTAG and pf14 armc2 ARMC2-3xTAG cells (n = 3) showed that recovery of the ARMC2-3xTAG was incomplete and plateaued after ~20 s suggesting a slow replacement of the bleached protein in the pool.
evidence: This is described in the results.

claim: After bleaching of the entire basal body-associated pool, IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG was interrupted for ~19 s.
source: After bleaching of the entire basal body-associated pool, IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG was interrupted for ~19 s (SD 7.7 s, n = 12, red bracket in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, top panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A similar average length of the gap was observed in the pf14 armc2 ARMC2-3xTAG strain (20 s).
source: A similar average length of the gap was observed in the pf14 armc2 ARMC2-3xTAG (20 s, SD 10.7 s, n = 18; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, bottom panel) suggesting that ARMC2 dynamics in the pool, that is, the rate by which it travels through the pool and attaches to IFT, are not altered by the absence of its cargo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ARMC2 dynamics in the pool are not altered by the absence of its cargo.
source: A similar average length of the gap was observed in the pf14 armc2 ARMC2-3xTAG (20 s, SD 10.7 s, n = 18; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, bottom panel) suggesting that ARMC2 dynamics in the pool, that is, the rate by which it travels through the pool and attaches to IFT, are not altered by the absence of its cargo.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar gap lengths in pf27 and pf14 armc2 backgrounds.

claim: After the gap, ARMC2-3xTAG traffic recommenced albeit at a reduced frequency.
source: After the gap, ARMC2-3xTAG traffic recommenced albeit at a reduced frequency in agreement with the incomplete recovery of the basal body signal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Considerably shorter gaps were observed for several IFT proteins (~6 s or less) and tubulin-GFP in similar bleaching experiments (~2 s).
source: Considerably shorter gaps were observed for several IFT proteins (~6 s or less) and tubulin-GFP in similar bleaching experiments (~2 s) (Wingfield et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: ARMC2-3xTAG dwells in the basal body-associated pool considerably longer than the IFT proteins of the train.
source: Thus, ARMC2-3xTAG dwells in the basal body-associated pool considerably longer than the IFT proteins of the train, which will carry it into the cilium, suggesting that IFT proteins and ARMC2 are recruited through different routes.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of dwell times.

claim: IFT proteins and ARMC2 are recruited through different routes.
source: Thus, ARMC2-3xTAG dwells in the basal body-associated pool considerably longer than the IFT proteins of the train, which will carry it into the cilium, suggesting that IFT proteins and ARMC2 are recruited through different routes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the different dwell times.

claim: IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG is frequently observed in short flagella but progressively decreases as flagella approach full length.
source: Similar to previous observations on the I1/f transport adapter IDA3 and several axonemal proteins (Wren et al., 2013; Craft et al., 2015; Hunter et al., 2018), IFT of ARMC2-3xTAG is frequently observed in short flagella but progressively decreases as flagella approach full length.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2 and 5 and supported by citations.

claim: The currently available cryo-EM structures of IFT trains were obtained by image averaging, which will cancel out signals from substoichiometric train components such as cargoes.
source: How axonemal proteins and their adapters are distributed onto the IFT trains remains unknown as the currently available cryo-EM structures of IFT trains were obtained by image averaging, which will cancel out signals from substoichiometric train components such as cargoes (Jordan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation and knowledge of cryo-EM methodology.

claim: In 35 regenerating armc2 ida3 ARMC2-mS IDA3-NG flagella analyzed over 905 s, 243 ARMC2-mS and 106 IDA3-NG particles moved anterogradely by IFT, of which 20 were cotransported on the same trains.
source: In 35 regenerating armc2 ida3 ARMC2-mS IDA3-NG flagella analyzed over 905 s, we observed 243 ARMC2-mS and 106 IDA3-NG particles moving anterogradely by IFT, of which 20 were cotransported on the same trains (Table 1).
evidence: This is quantified from two-color TIRF imaging and summarized in Table 1.

claim: For the oda3 armc2 oda6 ARMC2-mS ODA6-NG strain, 82 ARMC2-mS and 78 IC2-NG particles were observed in 20 flagella over 1575 s, of which three were cotransports.
source: For the oda3 armc2 oda6 ARMC2-mS ODA6-NG strain, we analyzed 20 flagella for 1575 s and observed 82 ARMC2-mS and 78 IC2-NG particles, of which three were cotransports (Table 1).
evidence: This is quantified from two-color TIRF imaging and summarized in Table 1.

claim: The observed probability that a train carries both ARMC2-mS and IDA3-NG was 0.022.
source: As anterograde IFT has a frequency of ~60 trains/min (Kozminski et al., 1993; Dentler, 2005; Engel et al., 2012; Reck et al., 2016), the observed probability that a train carries both cargoes was 0.022 for ARMC2-mS and IDA3-NG (i.e., ~2% of the trains carry ARMC2-mS and IDA3-NG) and 0.0019 for ARMC2-mS and IC2-NG.
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Table 1 and supported by citations for IFT frequency.

claim: The observed probability that a train carries both ARMC2-mS and IC2-NG was 0.0019.
source: As anterograde IFT has a frequency of ~60 trains/min (Kozminski et al., 1993; Dentler, 2005; Engel et al., 2012; Reck et al., 2016), the observed probability that a train carries both cargoes was 0.022 for ARMC2-mS and IDA3-NG (i.e., ~2% of the trains carry ARMC2-mS and IDA3-NG) and 0.0019 for ARMC2-mS and IC2-NG.
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Table 1 and supported by citations for IFT frequency.

claim: The observed probabilities of cotransport are close to the calculated probabilities if the two cargoes bind independently of each other to IFT trains.
source: These values are close to the calculated probabilities of 0.03 for the ARMC2-mS/IDA3-NG pair and 0.0026 for the ARMC2-mS/IC2-NG pair by which such cotransports would occur by chance if the two cargoes are transported independently of each other without a preference for a subclass of IFT trains (see Table 1 and Materials and methods for calculation).
evidence: This is calculated and compared to the observed values.

claim: ARMC2-mS and RSP3-NG were cotransported with a probability of 0.027 in full-length flagella significantly exceeding the value of 0.0023 calculated if these two proteins would attach independently of each other to the trains.
source: In contrast, RSP3-NG transport depends on ARMC2-mS and as expected ARMC2-mS and RSP3-NG were cotransported with a probability of 0.027 in full-length flagella significantly exceeding the value of 0.0023 calculated if these two proteins would attach independently of each other to the trains (Table 1).
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Table 1.

claim: ARMC2-mS, IDA3-NG, and IC2-NG are transported independently of each other.
source: In conclusion, ARMC2-mS, IDA3-NG, and IC2-NG are transported independently of each other arguing against a subclass of IFT trains specialized to carry axonemal proteins.
evidence: This is concluded from the cotransport analysis.

claim: The observations argue against a subclass of IFT trains specialized to carry axonemal proteins.
source: In conclusion, ARMC2-mS, IDA3-NG, and IC2-NG are transported independently of each other arguing against a subclass of IFT trains specialized to carry axonemal proteins.
evidence: This is concluded from the cotransport analysis.

source: Rather, the observations support a model, in which axonemal cargoes are stochastically distributed onto the IFT trains.
evidence: This is concluded from the cotransport analysis.

source: IFT adapters could be defined as a proteins or protein complexes, which facilitate IFT of a cargo (complex) without being necessary for either IFT itself or the functionality of the cargo once delivered into the cilium.

source: The transition zone, separating the cell body from the flagellum, functions as a diffusion barrier, which is thought to minimize or prevent the entry of large proteins and complexes into flagella by diffusion (Garcia-Gonzalo and Reiter, 2012; Kee et al., 2012).

source: Thus, the transition zone of Chlamydomonas might allow limited entry of RSs and ODAs in an IFT-independent manner in agreement with studies indicating diffusional entry of large proteins into primary cilia (Lin et al., 2013).

source: Mutations in mammalian Armc2 cause sperm malformations resulting in male infertility (Coutton et al., 2019).
